                                             PROJECT NO. 58481

 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                                 §       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                              §
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA § 37.0561                          §                      OF TEXAS


  JOINT COMMENTS OF WIND ENERGY TRANSMISSION TEXAS, LLC; CROSS
     TEXAS TRANSMISSION, LLC; LONE STAR TRANSMISSION, LLC; AND
SHARYLAND UTILITIES, L.L.C. ON THE PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF NEW
                             16 TAC § 25.194

       Wind Energy Transmission Texas, LLC (“WETT”); Cross Texas Transmission, LLC
(“CTT”); Lone Star Transmission, LLC (“Lone Star”); and Sharyland Utilities, L.L.C
(collectively, “Joint TSPs”) jointly submit these comments on the Proposal for Publication of new
16 Tex. Admin. Code (“TAC”) § 25.194. Per the Proposal for Publication, comments are due
April 17, 2026.1 Accordingly, these comments are timely filed.

       Joint TSPs are transmission-only transmission service providers (“TSPs”) who are required
to provide any needed transmission system upgrades to reliably serve transmission service
customers and, in turn, retail large load customers. Because Joint TSPs are often the lead contact
for large load customers interconnecting at transmission voltage for purposes of studying,
planning, and constructing the needed transmission investment, Joint TSPs are uniquely situated
to understand both the needs of large load customers and their impacts to the broader transmission
system.

                                              I.     Executive Summary
       Joint TSPs, like all stakeholders in this process, file these comments to help ensure that
large load customers in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, Inc. (“ERCOT”) region are
interconnected in a manner that minimizes the potential for stranded infrastructure costs, maintains
system reliability, and aligns with generally accepted cost causation principles. Central to the
intent of Senate Bill 6 (“SB 6”) is striking a proper balance between the incentives for large load
customers to site within ERCOT with ensuring the costs and impacts to the system are not
disproportionately borne by other retail customers. 2


       1
           Proposal for Publication of New 16 TAC § 25.194 at 4 (Mar. 12, 2026) (“Proposal for Publication”).
       2
           Tex. S. B. 6, 89th Leg., R.S. (2025).

                                                        1
        Joint TSPs appreciate the opportunity to participate in this proceeding and to assist in
formulating interconnection standards that best harmonize the language and intent of SB 6,3
existing state policy, and the practical realities of interconnecting large loads in Texas’ competitive
market. Accordingly, Joint TSPs offer the following suggestions to efficiently align market
incentives and cost causation principles:
            Intermediate Agreement and Interconnection Agreement – 16 TAC §§ 25.194(d) & (f)
                o The roles and responsibilities identified in Intermediate Agreements and
                  Interconnection Agreements should be assigned by Rule to the electric utility or
                  electric utilities making the relevant upgrades or providing the relevant
                  interconnection or services related thereto.
                o Utilities should be permitted to enter independent discretionary service
                  agreements directly with the retail load for collecting security and/or
                  contributions in aid of construction (“CIAC”) for the facilities they are
                  constructing or for any services being performed related thereto.
                o The rule should define a timeline by which the large load customer, TSP, and
                  distribution service provider (“DSP”) must enter an Intermediate Agreement
                  after the large load customer makes an interconnection request.
            Non-Refundable Interconnection Fee – 16 TAC § 25.194(f)(7)
                o A nonrefundable interconnection fee is inconsistent with statute, which requires
                  contributions paid by developers to be tied directly to needed facilities and trued
                  up to reflect actual costs.
                o Any interconnection fee that is applied as an offset to TSP rate base is unduly
                  punitive to TSPs, and in some instances may offset rate base by over 100%,
                  unlawfully taking investment.
                o To the extent the Commission wishes large load interconnection customers to
                  contribute to reducing the transmission costs of other retail customers, Joint
                  TSPs propose potential alternatives wherein large load customers might pay a
                  fee toward:
                            ERCOT-wide wholesale transmission service 4CP rates, to be applied
                             across DSPs annually; or
                            TSP credit riders.
            Contribution In Aid of Construction – 16 TAC § 25.194(f)(9)
                o The final rule should provide additional clarity regarding the definition of “direct
                  interconnection costs” to avoid unintended consequences.
                o In order to preserve rate base incentives, the rule should permit the payment over
                  time of any larger networked transmission upgrades.

       3
           Senate Bill 6 §§ 1-2 (codified at PURA §§ 35.004, 37.0561).

                                                        2
           Proposed redlines to the Proposal for Publication are provided as Attachment A.
                   II.     Intermediate Agreement & Interconnection Agreement –
                                            16 TAC §§ 25.194(d) & (f)
       Joint TSPs are not opposed to the three-party arrangement described between a large load
customer, the interconnecting DSP, and the interconnecting TSP, and appreciate the flexibility in
contracting described in the Proposal for Publication. Joint TSPs respectfully recommend three
adjustments to better effect the intended flexibility while avoiding needless disputes.
       First, the final rule should ensure the roles and responsibilities outlined in §§ 25.194(d)(1)-
(11) and (f)(1)-(10) are assigned to the utility responsible for providing the applicable
interconnection or making the applicable upgrade. For example, if an interconnecting TSP must
procure significant equipment or services for the interconnection, or construct significant facilities
interconnecting to its system, the financial security outlined in § 25.194(d)(11) should be collected
directly by the TSP. In any final rule, the Commission also should clarify that the TSP whose
system connects the customer to the bulk electric grid is the “Interconnecting TSP” for purposes
of relevant agreements. Aligning contractual roles with the existing responsibilities of DSPs and
TSPs ensures both efficiency and consistency across utilities.
       To provide context, when the interconnecting TSP and interconnecting DSP are different
utilities, it is very often the case that the TSP conducts the vast majority of the construction and
upgrade work (perhaps upwards of 90%) to interconnect the large load customer to its existing
transmission system, whereas the DSP may be responsible for a relatively smaller portion of the
project, such as new facilities related to metering and direct retail services. Thus, it is more
efficient and makes practical sense for the TSP to be the entity to directly collect the security from
the large load customer, particularly when the new rule specifically contemplates agreements
between the TSP and the large load customer.
       This general concept regarding the interconnecting TSP’s substantial and direct
interconnection role appears to already be contemplated in proposed § 25.194(d)(9), which
appropriately provides that the interconnecting TSP may be the entity to directly collect the study
fee from the large load customer. This makes practical sense as, again, such TSPs often lead the
efforts of studying, planning, and constructing the needed expansion on their existing transmission
systems, and are uniquely situated to understand both the needs of large loads and the resulting
impacts to the system.


                                                  3
         Second, the rule should allow utilities to enter independent discretionary services
agreements directly with the large load customers rather than three-party agreements, should they
choose. In some instances, TSPs or DSPs might prefer to enter a two-party service agreement for
collecting security or CIACs for the facilities they are constructing, or for any services being
performed such as the ERCOT Large Load Interconnection Study. Allowing utilities to enter
either the three-party arrangement described in the Proposal for Publication or a more traditional
two-party arrangement provides additional flexibility, promotes efficiency in contracting, and
could avoid protracted disputes among the entities. In any final rule, the Joint TSPs also request
the Commission to clarify that interconnecting TSPs have the right to contract directly with large
load interconnection customers.
        Lastly, the rule should delineate a clear timeline for entering an Intermediate Agreement,
just as the Proposal for Publication includes various timelines for events after executing the
Agreement. The same deadline for entering an Intermediate Agreement should apply regardless
of whether the request for interconnection is made through the DSP or TSP. This would help
reduce delays to interconnecting large loads with valid requests.

                III.    Non-Refundable Interconnection Fee – 16 TAC § 25.194(f)(7)
        16 TAC § 25.194(f)(7) proposes a non-refundable interconnection fee of $50,000 per MW
of contracted peak demand, and then further proposes requiring the interconnecting TSP to use
that amount to offset its rate base. Joint TSPs propose removing this provision. An interconnection
fee that has no basis in actual costs or cost causation is (a) against generally-accepted ratemaking
principles, (b) unlawfully takes investment from utilities, and (c) directly contradicts the
framework outlined by the legislature in SB 6, which requires refund or true-up to actual expense.
As other commenters have noted, it could also disincentivize large loads from locating in ERCOT.
Joint TSPs recognize that such a mechanism may be intended to protect non-large-load retail
customers. As Joint TSPs noted in comments filed in Project No. 58480 on October 31, 2025, the
best means of ensuring large load customers pay their fair share of transmission costs is through
the retail cost allocation and rate design process.
        If the Commission decides to impose a non-cost-based interconnection fee, it should be
applied for the protection of retail customers without unintentionally harming TSPs’ financial
stability.


                                                  4
    1. A nonrefundable interconnection fee is inconsistent with statute.
          A nonrefundable dollar-per-megawatt interconnection fee is at odds with SB 6’s outlined
methods of acceptable requirements for financial commitment. SB 6 considers: (1) a dollar-per-
megawatt security which “must be refunded, in whole or in part, after the security is applied to any
outstanding amounts owed;”4 (2) CIAC,5 which is tied to actual construction costs; or, (3) security
for specific significant equipment or services. 6 Each of these methods are based on actual costs of
interconnection and subject to true-up should the financial commitment exceed actual costs, as
opposed to an interconnection fee.
   2. Any interconnection fee that is applied as an offset to rate base is unduly punitive to
       TSPs.
          A non-refundable interconnection fee, if applied as an offset to rate base, would
detrimentally impact TSP investment unrelated to the interconnection of large load customers.
PURA requires an opportunity to earn a reasonable return as the compensation for constructing,
owning, and operating transmission investment in Texas. The interconnection fee, if applied in
the manner as currently proposed, eliminates the opportunity to earn a return on regulated
investment.
          The non-refundable interconnection fee would financially disincentivize TSPs from
interconnecting these large load customers. The impact to rate base is particularly detrimental for
relatively smaller TSPs, such as the Joint TSPs. For example, one of the Joint TSPs is the smallest
investor-owned utility in Texas. Nonetheless, that TSP is often approached about interconnecting
large load customers, including proposed loads exceeding 1 GW, given the ideal location of its
existing transmission system, which is near a heavy industrial center. Assume a situation in which
a 2-GW load paid this fee to this TSP at an amount of $100 million, as proposed. All else equal,
that would result in a more than 30% reduction to that TSP’s rate base and return on investment,
along with a 12% reduction to its approved revenue requirement. This would effectively reduce
the TSP’s weighted average return on capital by more than 200 basis points, which could
negatively impact the TSP’s ability to attract future capital and make future investment in its
system.     Furthermore, this would reduce Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation,

       4
           Senate Bill 6 § 1 (codified at PURA § 35.004(h)(1), (i)).
       5
           Senate Bill 6 § 1 (codified at PURA § 35.004(h)(2)).
       6
           Senate Bill 6 § 1 (codified at PURA § 35.004(h)(3)).

                                                          5
 and Amortization (“EBITDA”) and Funds From Operations (“FFO”), negatively impacting credit
metrics prospectively and increasing cost of debt.
    3. Alternative options exist to facilitate large load customer contributions to system
        interconnection costs.
         To the extent the Commission wishes to use a nonrefundable interconnection fee that does
not correspond to investment or expense and is intended to ensure large load customers contribute
toward reducing transmission costs, alternative methods exist that both benefit retail customers
more directly and avoid the unintended consequence of penalizing interconnecting utilities.
              a. Payment Toward Wholesale Transmission Costs
        First, large load customers might pay a flat fee to be applied to ERCOT-wide wholesale
transmission costs. These fees could be credited to other retail customers across the four coincident
peak transmission charge matrix.7 Such a credit would ensure that large load customers contribute
toward system upgrade costs, that the benefit is applied directly to retail customers, and that TSPs
are not unintentionally harmed by large offsets to rate base. Additionally, because the balance
may be changed from year to year in a single annual proceeding, it should not impose a heavy
administrative burden on the Commission.
              b. Payment Applied Through TSP Credit Riders
         Second, large load customers might pay a fee to be credited directly to retail customers
through a TSP Wholesale Transmission Tariff Credit Rider amortized across a period of time
approved by the Commission. This credit would flow through directly to other retail customers—
alleviating rate shock from rapid transmission infrastructure growth across the state—without
reducing TSPs’ opportunity to earn a return on investments.

                    IV.      Contribution In Aid of Construction – 16 TAC § 25.194(f)(9)
         Joint TSPs appreciate SB 6’s mandate to minimize the potential for stranded and
underutilized transmission assets, and support a CIAC for direct costs of interconnection. 8 Further,
in addition to those methods listed above, CIAC may provide an opportunity for large load
customers to contribute toward system upgrade costs. However, any method using CIAC to


        7
           The Commission is currently conducting an evaluation of the four coincident peak as the method of
transmission cost recovery. Evaluation of Transmission Cost Recovery, Project No. 58484 (pending).
        8
            Senate Bill 6 § 2 (codified at PURA § 37.0561).

                                                         6
 recover direct interconnection costs should ensure TSPs’ ability to earn a return both of and on
those capital investments.
    1. “Direct interconnection costs” should be clearly defined.
        Joint TSPs respectfully request that the final rule clearly define the “direct interconnection
costs” to be paid for by CIAC. As drafted, 16 TAC § 25.194(f)(9)(A) would allow “direct
interconnection costs” to include broader system upgrade costs in addition to those costs that are
traditionally considered “direct.” Specifically, direct interconnection costs should be defined as
radial transmission line extensions and any necessary bay at the first station needed to interconnect
the customer to the transmission system. These are the facilities that are needed to serve only the
new interconnecting large load and should therefore be borne by only the new interconnecting
large load itself.
        Further, direct interconnection costs should explicitly exclude system upgrades that may
be only incidentally triggered by a large load, including networked transmission lines or
reinforcements that become part of the ERCOT networked grid. Such costs serve and benefit the
broader transmission network rather than a single interconnection. The interconnecting load does
not benefit from such investment to any greater degree than any other transmission customer, and
such investments are traditionally not imposed on individual customers. Recovering system
upgrade costs through Transmission Cost of Service (“TCOS”) proceedings is consistent with
historical practices and ensures individual customers are not overcharged.
        Lastly, a clear definition will reduce regulatory uncertainty and the potential for both
under-recovery and stranded investments, not to mention reduce inconsistencies across utilities in
ERCOT as is currently the case. The Commission has been charged by the legislature to “support
business development in this state.” As many stakeholders have articulated, regulatory uncertainty
greatly disincentivizes large load developers from citing in Texas. As such, providing a clear
definition of “direct interconnection costs” honors the intent of the legislature and of the statute
governing this rulemaking.
    2. Efficient funding and recovery of TSP capital investments in system upgrades.
        In the alternative, the Commission might ensure existing customers are protected from the
costs of new load by explicitly linking cost responsibility to rate impacts via a targeted
transmission charge that is paid over time and includes a return on the TSP’s investment. Under
this construct used in other jurisdictions, a large load would pay standard transmission rates so


                                                  7
 long as the transmission revenues associated with serving that load are sufficient to cover the
incremental transmission revenue requirement created by the associated system upgrades. If, after
accounting for the new load’s transmission revenues, existing customers would otherwise
experience an increase in average transmission rates, the large load would be responsible for the
difference in order to hold existing customers harmless.
         To address the risk that a large load may not materialize as forecast, or subsequently
reduces demand, this framework could be paired with contractual commitments from the large
load, including take or pay obligations and appropriate security. 9 These mechanisms would ensure
that the transmission revenue requirement associated with network upgrades built to serve the load
continues to be met even if actual usage falls short, thereby protecting existing customers from
stranded cost risk.
         A framework that requires large loads to fund direct interconnection facilities, explicitly
tests and preserves rate neutrality for existing customers, and relies on contractual commitments
and security to manage load risk would closely align SB 6 and ERCOT’s historical practices.

                                                   V.        Conclusion
        Joint TSPs appreciate the opportunity to contribute in this project and look forward to
working with Staff and stakeholders towards the effective implementation of SB 6’s requirements.


                                                     Respectfully submitted,




        9
            This approach has clear analogs elsewhere. In Illinois, ComEd has implemented transmission security
and revenue commitment arrangements tied to FERC jurisdictional transmission service. Under those arrangements,
transmission facilities remain network assets recovered through transmission rates, while large load customers
provide revenue guarantees to prevent rate impacts to other customers if load does not fully materialize. Similarly,
Ameren Missouri has obtained approval from the Missouri Public Service Commission for large load frameworks
that rely on minimum billing, long term commitments, and security to ensure rate neutrality for existing customers
while allowing utility ownership of long-lived system assets.

April 17,2026.1 Accordingly, these comments are timely filed.

          Joint TSPs are transmission-only transmission service providers ("TSPs") who are required
to provide any needed transmission system upgrades to reliably serve transmission service
customers and, in turn, retail large load customers. Because Joint TSPs are often the lead contact
for large load customers interconnecting at transmission voltage for purposes of studying,
planning, and constructing the needed transmission investment, Joint TSPs are uniquely situated
to understand both the needs of large load customers and their impacts to the broader transmission
system.

                                               I.     Executive Summary
          Joint TSPs, like all stakeholders in this process, file these comments to help ensure that
large load customers in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, Inc. ("ERCOT") region are
interconnected in a manner that minimizes the potential for stranded infrastructure costs, maintains
system reliability, and aligns with generally accepted cost causation principles. Central to the
intent of Senate Bill 6 ("SB 6") is striking a proper balance between the incentives for large load
customers to site within ERCOT with ensuring the costs and impacts to the system are not
disproportionately borne by other retail customers. 2

                   II.     Intermediate Agreement & Interconnection Agreement -
                                            16 TAC §§25.194(d) & (f)
       Joint TSPs are not opposed to the three-party arrangement described between a large load
customer, the interconnecting DSP, and the interconnecting TSP, and appreciate the flexibility in
contracting described in the Proposal for Publication. Joint TSPs respectfully recommend three
adjustments to better effect the intended flexibility while avoiding needless disputes.
       First, the final rule should ensure the roles and responsibilities outlined in §§ 25.194(d)(1)-
(11) and (f)(1)-(10) are assigned to the utility responsible for providing the applicable
interconnection or making the applicable upgrade. For example, if an interconnecting TSP must
procure significant equipment or services for the interconnection, or construct significant facilities
interconnecting to its system, the financial security outlined in § 25.194(d)(11) should be collected
directly by the TSP. In any final rule, the Commission also should clarify that the TSP whose
system connects the customer to the bulk electric grid is the "Interconnecting TSP" for purposes
of relevant agreements. Aligning contractual roles with the existing responsibilities ofDSPs and
TSPs ensures both efficiency and consistency across utilities.
       To provide context, when the interconnecting TSP and interconnecting DSP are different
utilities, it is very often the case that the TSP conducts the vast maj ority of the construction and
upgrade work (perhaps upwards of 90%) to interconnect the large load customer to its existing
transmission system, whereas the DSP may be responsible for a relatively smaller portion of the
project, such as new facilities related to metering and direct retail services.     Thus, it is more
efficient and makes practical sense for the TSP to be the entity to directly collect the security from
the large load customer, particularly when the new rule specifically contemplates agreements
between the TSP and the large load customer.
       This general concept regarding the interconnecting TSP' s substantial and direct
interconnection role appears to already be contemplated in proposed § 25.194(d)(9), which
appropriately provides that the interconnecting TSP may be the entity to directly collect the study
fee from the large load customer. This makes practical sense as, again, such TSPs often lead the
efforts of studying, planning, and constructing the needed expansion on their existing transmission
systems, and are uniquely situated to understand both the needs of large loads and the resulting
impacts to the system.

          Second, the rule should allow utilities to enter independent discretionary services
agreements directly with the large load customers rather than three-party agreements, should they
choose. In some instances, TSPs or DSPs might prefer to enter a two-party service agreement for
collecting security or CIACs for the facilities they are constructing, or for any services being
performed such as the ERCOT Large Load Interconnection Study. Allowing utilities to enter
either the three-party arrangement described in the Proposal for Publication or a more traditional
two-party arrangement provides additional flexibility, promotes efficiency in contracting, and
could avoid protracted disputes among the entities. In any final rule, the Joint TSPs also request
the Commission to clarify that interconnecting TSPs have the right to contract directly with large
load interconnection customers.
        Lastly, the rule should delineate a clear timeline for entering an Intermediate Agreement,
just as the Proposal for Publication includes various timelines for events after executing the
Agreement. The same deadline for entering an Intermediate Agreement should apply regardless
of whether the request for interconnection is made through the DSP or TSP. This would help
reduce delays to interconnecting large loads with valid requests.

                 III.    Non-Refundable Interconnection Fee - 16 TAC §25.194(f)(7)
         16 TAC § 25.194(f)(7) proposes a non-refundable interconnection fee of $50,000 per MW
of contracted peak demand, and then further proposes requiring the interconnecting TSP to use
that amount to offset its rate base. Joint TSPs propose removing this provision. An interconnection
fee that has no basis in actual costs or cost causation is (a) against generally-accepted ratemaking
principles, (b) unlawfully takes investment from utilities, and (c) directly contradicts the
framework outlined by the legislature in SB 6, which requires refund or true-up to actual expense.
As other commenters have noted, it could also disincentivize large loads from locating in ERCOT.
Joint TSPs recognize that such a mechanism may be intended to protect non-large-load retail
customers. As Joint TSPs noted in comments filed in Project No. 58480 on October 31, 2025, the
best means of ensuring large load customers pay their fair share of transmission costs is through
the retail cost allocation and rate design process.
         If the Commission decides to impose a non-cost-based interconnection fee, it should be
applied for the protection of retail customers without unintentionally harming TSPs' financial
stability.


                                                      4
     1. A nonrefundable interconnection fee is inconsistent with statute.
          A nonrefundable dollar-per-megawatt interconnection fee is at odds with SB 6's outlined
methods of acceptable requirements for financial commitment. SB 6 considers: (1) a dollar-per-
megawatt security which "must be refunded, in whole or in part, after the security is applied to any
outstanding amounts owed,"4 (2) CIAC,5 which is tied to actual construction costs; or, (3) security
for specific significant equipment or services.6 Each of these methods are based on actual costs of
interconnection and subj ect to true-up should the financial commitment exceed actual costs, as
opposed to an interconnection fee.
   2. Any interconnection fee that is applied as an offset to rate base is unduly punitive to
          TSPs.
          A non-refundable interconnection fee, if applied as an offset to rate base, would
detrimentally impact TSP investment unrelated to the interconnection of large load customers.
PURA requires an opportunity to earn a reasonable return as the compensation for constructing,
owning, and operating transmission investment in Texas. The interconnection fee, if applied in
the manner as currently proposed, eliminates the opportunity to earn a return on regulated
investment.
          The non-refundable interconnection fee would financially disincentivize TSPs from
interconnecting these large load customers. The impact to rate base is particularly detrimental for
relatively smaller TSPs, such as the Joint TSPs. For example, one ofthe Joint TSPs is the smallest
investor-owned utility in Texas. Nonetheless, that TSP is often approached about interconnecting
large load customers, including proposed loads exceeding 1 GW, given the ideal location of its
existing transmission system, which is near a heavy industrial center. Assume a situation in which
a 2-GW load paid this fee to this TSP at an amount of $100 million, as proposed. All else equal,
that would result in a more than 30% reduction to that TSP' s rate base and return on investment,
along with a 12% reduction to its approved revenue requirement. This would effectively reduce
the TSP' s weighted average return on capital by more than 200 basis points, which could
negatively impact the TSP' s ability to attract future capital and make future investment in its
system.      Furthermore, this would reduce Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation,

    3. Alternative options exist to facilitate large load customer contributions to system
        interconnection costs.
         To the extent the Commission wishes to use a nonrefundable interconnection fee that does
not correspond to investment or expense and is intended to ensure large load customers contribute
toward reducing transmission costs, alternative methods exist that both benefit retail customers
more directly and avoid the unintended consequence of penalizing interconnecting utilities.
             a. Payment Toward Wholesale Transmission Costs
        First, large load customers might pay a flat fee to be applied to ERCOT-wide wholesale
transmission costs. These fees could be credited to other retail customers across the four coincident
peak transmission charge matrix.7 Such a credit would ensure that large load customers contribute
toward system upgrade costs, that the benefit is applied directly to retail customers, and that TSPs
are not unintentionally harmed by large offsets to rate base. Additionally, because the balance
may be changed from year to year in a single annual proceeding, it should not impose a heavy
administrative burden on the Commission.
             b. Payment Applied Through TSP Credit Riders
         Second, large load customers might pay a fee to be credited directly to retail customers
through a TSP Wholesale Transmission Tariff Credit Rider amortized across a period of time
approved by the Commission. This credit would flow through directly to other retail customers-
alleviating rate shock from rapid transmission infrastructure growth across the state-without
reducing TSPs' opportunity to earn a return on investments.

underutilized transmission assets, and support a CIAC for direct costs of interconnection. 8 Further,
in addition to those methods listed above, CIAC may provide an opportunity for large load
customers to contribute toward system upgrade costs. However, any method using CIAC to

    1. "Direct interconnection costs" should be clearly defined.
        Joint TSPs respectfully request that the final rule clearly define the "direct interconnection
costs" to be paid for by CIAC.      As drafted, 16 TAC § 25.194(f)(9)(A) would allow "direct
interconnection costs" to include broader system upgrade costs in addition to those costs that are
traditionally considered "direct." Specifically, direct interconnection costs should be defined as
radial transmission line extensions and any necessary bay at the first station needed to interconnect
the customer to the transmission system. These are the facilities that are needed to serve only the
new interconnecting large load and should therefore be borne by only the new interconnecting
large load itself.
        Further, direct interconnection costs should explicitly exclude system upgrades that may
be only incidentally triggered by a large load, including networked transmission lines or
reinforcements that become part of the ERCOT networked grid. Such costs serve and benefit the
broader transmission network rather than a single interconnection. The interconnecting load does
not benefit from such investment to any greater degree than any other transmission customer, and
such investments are traditionally not imposed on individual customers.          Recovering system
upgrade costs through Transmission Cost of Service ("TCOS") proceedings is consistent with
historical practices and ensures individual customers are not overcharged.
        Lastly, a clear definition will reduce regulatory uncertainty and the potential for both
under-recovery and stranded investments, not to mention reduce inconsistencies across utilities in
ERCOT as is currently the case. The Commission has been charged by the legislature to "support
business development in this state." As many stakeholders have articulated, regulatory uncertainty
greatly disincentivizes large load developers from citing in Texas. As such, providing a clear
definition of "direct interconnection costs" honors the intent of the legislature and of the statute
governing this rulemaking.
    2. Efficient funding and recovery of TSP capital investments in system upgrades.
        In the alternative, the Commission might ensure existing customers are protected from the
costs of new load by explicitly linking cost responsibility to rate impacts via a targeted
transmission charge that is paid over time and includes a return on the TSP' s investment. Under
this construct used in other jurisdictions, a large load would pay standard transmission rates so


                                                  7
 long as the transmission revenues associated with serving that load are sufficient to cover the
incremental transmission revenue requirement created by the associated system upgrades. If, after
accounting for the new load' s transmission revenues, existing customers would otherwise
experience an increase in average transmission rates, the large load would be responsible for the
difference in order to hold existing customers harmless.
         To address the risk that a large load may not materialize as forecast, or subsequently
reduces demand, this framework could be paired with contractual commitments from the large
load, including take or pay obligations and appropriate security: These mechanisms would ensure
that the transmission revenue requirement associated with network upgrades built to serve the load
continues to be met even if actual usage falls short, thereby protecting existing customers from
stranded cost risk.
         A framework that requires large loads to fund direct interconnection facilities, explicitly
tests and preserves rate neutrality for existing customers, and relies on contractual commitments
and security to manage load risk would closely align SB 6 and ERCOT' s historical practices.

         Joint TSPs appreciate the opportunity to contribute in this project and look forward to
working with Staff and stakeholders towards the effective implementation of SB 6's requirements.
